questions.question: Working from the surface to the centre, describe the earth's internal structure, naming each layer and boundary and giving each layer's approximate depth, composition and physical state.
questions.expected_answer: The crust is the rigid outer shell of silicate rock, from the surface to between about 5 and 70 kilometres, and it is solid; its base is the Mohorovičić discontinuity, or Moho, where seismic waves abruptly speed up. The mantle extends from the Moho to about 2 900 kilometres and consists of solid iron- and magnesium-rich silicate rock, mostly peridotite, making up roughly 84 per cent of the earth's volume. Within its upper part, from about 100 to 250 kilometres, the asthenosphere sits so close to its melting point that it creeps plastically, which permits plate movement. The Gutenberg discontinuity at about 2 900 kilometres marks the top of the iron-nickel core. The outer core, to about 5 150 kilometres, is liquid, and its churning generates the magnetic field. Below the Lehmann discontinuity the inner core, reaching the centre at 6 371 kilometres, is solid despite temperatures of 5 000 to 6 000 degrees Celsius, because immense pressure keeps the iron solid. Temperature, pressure and density all increase with depth.

questions.question: Contrast continental and oceanic crust under the headings thickness, composition, density and age, and use the density contrast to explain what happens where the two converge.
questions.expected_answer: Continental crust, or sial, is 30 to 50 kilometres thick and up to 70 beneath major mountain belts; it is granitic, light at about 2,7 grams per cubic centimetre, and extremely old — the Makhonjwa Mountains near Barberton contain rocks over three billion years old. Oceanic crust, or sima, is only 5 to 10 kilometres thick, basaltic, denser at about 3,0 grams per cubic centimetre, and young: no ocean floor exceeds roughly 200 million years, because it is continuously created at mid-ocean ridges and consumed at subduction zones. Where the two converge, the denser oceanic slab sinks beneath the lighter continental crust — subduction — which is simply buoyancy at work, and it explains why deep ocean trenches lie along continental margins. A further distinction is that a tectonic plate is lithosphere, the crust plus the rigid uppermost mantle, about 100 kilometres thick, riding on the plastic asthenosphere.

questions.question: No borehole has passed much beyond twelve kilometres. Explain, using seismic waves and the shadow zones, how the states of the outer and inner core were established, and add the supporting evidence.
questions.expected_answer: Large earthquakes send body waves through the whole planet. P-waves are compressional, fastest, and cross solids, liquids and gases; S-waves are transverse and cannot cross a liquid, because liquid has no rigidity to transmit a sideways shear. Seismic stations worldwide show that beyond about 103 degrees from the epicentre S-waves never arrive at all — an S-wave shadow zone. Their complete absence proves they met a liquid layer, so the outer core is molten. P-waves do cross, but are sharply refracted where they enter the liquid core, creating a P-wave shadow zone between about 103 and 143 degrees; the width of that band fixes the depth of the core-mantle boundary. Faint P-wave arrivals inside the shadow zone, bent again at the Lehmann discontinuity, reveal a solid inner core. Supporting evidence: the earth's average density of about 5,5 grams per cubic centimetre far exceeds the 2,7 of surface rock, pointing to a metallic interior; the magnetic field requires circulating liquid metal; and iron meteorites, thought to be fragments of shattered planetary cores, match the required iron-nickel composition.
